Interface design

Nearly Every Button on the Internet Does the Same Thing

We read 3,379 button components from 312 public libraries. 96 percent of them commit on a single press. The rest, a few dozen holds, slides and confirmations, show what else a button can be.

By the organism generator · Data from shadcn's public registry directory, read on Nov. 20, 2026

A button has one job: to turn a decision into an action. How it does that job is a design choice, and it says something. A plain press is quick and forgiving. A button you have to hold, or drag across, slows you down on purpose, so nobody pays or deletes by accident.

To see which choices designers actually make, we collected every button-like part in shadcn's directory of component registries, the libraries that developers copy into their own products, and read each one's source code. After folding in duplicates and setting aside example files, 3,379 distinct buttons remained, about 863 thousand lines of code.

The rare, deliberate buttons

Only 142 buttons ask for more than a press. They are rare because they cost the user time, and that cost is the point: each one is built for a moment when a mistake would hurt.

Most buttons bounce, a little

440 of the buttons state the physics of their motion as a spring. From each spring's stiffness, damping and mass we worked out two things a person feels: whether it overshoots (its damping ratio; below 1 it does), and how long it takes to settle. The typical spring has a damping ratio of 0.82. That is just enough overshoot to feel alive, settling in about a quarter of a second.

What they add on top

Two in three buttons are plain. The rest add a visual idea to the press: a glow, a blur, an icon that reshapes as it works, a liquid fill, a shimmer that sweeps across the label. Select a trick to see every button that uses it.

Visual tricks, by number of buttons

A button can use several.

What they forget

Motion that delights one person can make another dizzy, and a button that only answers a mouse shuts out anyone using a keyboard. The census shows how often these are handled, and how often a library paints its own colors in a way that a product's theme cannot reach.

How we did this

We started from shadcn's public directory of component registries (593 listed). From every registry marked healthy or degraded, we read its index and kept parts whose name, title or description describe a button (including calls to action, hold-to-confirm, slide-to-confirm and confirmation buttons), leaving out range sliders and whole page sections. We downloaded each part's source as a developer installing it would.

A program read each part's code, with comments removed, into fixed fields: what drives it (a press, a drag, a held time, a state or the pointer's distance), how it commits, the words' behavior while it acts, its visual tricks, its springs, whether it handles reduced motion and the keyboard, and the colors it writes out by hand. Each value keeps the line of code it was read from; select a row in the table to see them. Parts published by more than one registry were counted once (972 copies were folded in) and example files were set aside.

The census has limits. Its accuracy has not yet been measured against a hand-checked sample, and pattern-reading misses things: one button described as asking for confirmation is recorded as a plain press. About half the parts only mention a button in their description. Timings come from code, not from watching the buttons move. The libraries are the shadcn ecosystem, which shares a look and is not every button on the web.
